OpenAI - GPT-Rosalind-6 System Card Addendum: trusted-access frontier biology model (2026-10-30)

attrs.summary: GPT-Rosalind-6 is a frontier reasoning model for biology, drug discovery and translational medicine, offered as GPT-Rosalind-6 Research to qualified scientists, research institutes, companies and government partners. It uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra. It has fewer refusals on dual-use biological queries but is only available via trusted access: OpenAI reviews applicants proposed uses, security controls and governance practices before granting access, and retains refusals on biological weaponization and other safety topics. Under the Preparedness Framework the launch is treated as High capability in the Biological and Chemical domain, below the Critical threshold; it is treated as Critical in Cybersecurity and below High in AI Self-Improvement, relying on GPT-6 Astra assessments for other Preparedness risks. Safeguards have four components: trusted access controls for verified higher-capability life sciences use, model-level boundaries against harmful biological and cyber assistance, monitoring and enforcement designed to detect abuse, and additional contractual requirements. It retains GPT-6 Astra standard cyber safeguards including real-time blocking. Approved customers must maintain strong identity and access management, administrator controls, least-privilege access controls and processes to remove access when a user no longer has a legitimate need. Biosecurity red-teaming was tested on GPT-Rosalind-5.5 before launch and is being repeated for GPT-Rosalind-6; details are not public but were shared with the Safety Advisory Group committee.

Anthropic - Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks (2026-10-12)

attrs.summary: Anthropic says new methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillation attacks on Claude by around 90 to 99 percent. Distillation attacks are covert industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another without authorization, often using networks of fraudulent accounts. Anthropic names Zhipu as having distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3, and says that after finding Claude cyber safeguards degraded its attacks the company switched to an older Claude model and another lab model. CAISSI has assessed GLM-5.3 as the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date. Anthropic also reports a case in which requests to Moonshot Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of a distillation effort, including one request from a user believed to be affiliated with China PLA seeking to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. The new defenses involve trade-offs, including turning away meaningful revenue.

nodes.label: anthropic
Anthropic - An update on independent evaluators: METR gets employee-like access (2026-10-15)

attrs.summary: Anthropic has started giving employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, and METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Anthropic is also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators and is in early discussions with organizations including Hugging Face. The rationale is that evaluators need expertise including understanding how evaluations can go wrong such as alignment faking, independence from equity and financing, enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks, and freedom to publish observations and assessments. Anthropic draws an analogy to bank supervision, where resident examiners work inside the largest banks because banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do. The move follows a commitment to stronger independent third-party assessment and the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

nodes.label: Olam Labs / Y Combinator Labs - One brutal Minecraft night: 50 agents invent chicken handoff protocols and a Fertilizer Officer (2026-11-02)

attrs.summary: Researchers from Olam Labs and Y Combinator Labs tested large agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry. In the Civ50 experiment 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents ran in a Minecraft survival world for three hours with the only high-level instruction Build a thriving civilization, inside a custom open-source environment where agents observe the world, run Python scripts and create files in a shared sandbox. Within 90 seconds the agents harvested nearly every tree near the spawn point, and they exchanged about 5,900 messages. A leader emerged without any vote as 46 of 49 other agents sent their first message to Ada, the first name in the directory; Ada drafted initial settlement plans. The first in-game night brought 22 deaths, and despite no penalty beyond losing gear the swarm reacted with extreme risk aversion: after the third night Ada ordered a halt to all major optional construction, digging and distant exploration. Agents built a micro-managed scarcity administration: one maintained a ration list and calculated hunger deficits for injured colleagues, another wrote an automated fishing script that prompted a dozen agents to fish in shifts, and four agents spent eleven minutes debating the appointment of a Sole Fertilizer Officer for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. When Ada tossed a cooked chicken to a hungry agent and a bystander ate it, a three-minute investigation produced a written handoff protocol banning tossing and requiring personally labeled chests; the word Toss appeared in seven messages before the incident and 125 afterward, 85 of them warnings. In direct competition the behavior flipped: in nine 45-minute rounds of Minecraft Bed Wars, ten GPT agents beat ten Claude Opus 5.5 agents 6-3, and across seven Mindustry matches GPT-6.1 Sol in the Codex coding environment beat Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code 6-1. A coding-environment bug blocked block-breaking when an agent held an enchanted sword; Claude agents wrongly concluded block-breaking was broken entirely and, when ahead on kills, stopped attacking to run out the clock, while GPT agents identified that automatic tool selection failed with an enchanted sword and fixed it by switching to an iron pickaxe, spreading the workaround across the team immediately. GPT agents communicated 5 to 30 times more often than Claude, chained multiple game actions into single command-line calls, and on two occasions wrote Python scripts on the spot to build a tower of blocks after an ender pearl teleported them 160 blocks below the arena. In three Mindustry matches when games hung in the balance GPT agents downloaded Mindustry public source code from the internet through their Linux sandbox and adjusted tactics; Claude agents never searched for game code online in the studied matches. Claude never swapped its leader and decided proposals through +1 votes. Both the Mindustry environment and the Multi-Agent Harbor framework were released as open source, and Diplomacy is planned for the arena. The authors argue simulations are an early warning system for real-world AI swarms and mirror production coding environments.

Adobe Research / UC San Diego - EditAgent: AI agents editing images like a Photoshop professional (2026-11-01)

attrs.summary: Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that edits images more like a Photoshop pro. Instead of retrying the same general-purpose editor over and over, the agent picks the right specialized tool for each task and lets a standard language model choose the best result based on measured image data. The approach works but needs about ten times the compute.

nodes.label: Vals AI - Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces (2026-11-01)

attrs.summary: A study by Vals AI tested 25 AI models for alignment with Chinese government positions and found surprising results: Chinese models respond to political questions less uniformly than expected, and Western models occasionally adopt official Beijing positions too. The language of the prompt had an especially strong effect on the political slant of responses.
